source: Taatgen, Huss, Dickison & Anderson (2008) The acquisition of robust and flexible cognitive skills
finding: Production compilation is defined as: when two productions fire in sequence they merge into one new production; a fact retrieved by the first is written into the new rule. This removes the retrieve-and-check cycle, giving speedup and fewer errors. The authors rank it as the main learning mechanism in their model.
numbers: Mechanism example (Table 3): retrieve-operator rule + press-key rule + retrieved operator -> one rule that recognises the state and presses the key. Grain size: instance theory specialises whole problems, chunking sub-tasks, compilation single steps.
quote: if two productions fire in sequence, they are combined into a single new production that is added to procedural memory
limits: Compilation only speeds up knowledge already present; it needs a working slow procedure first.
agent_relevance: Lesson to routine: a slow instruction-following pass must exist and succeed before it can be folded into a fast rule.

source: Taatgen et al. (2008) Experiment 1: list vs context instructions in a flight-management task
finding: Instructions that stated pre- and post-conditions (context) beat plain numbered step lists, mostly on hard problems that needed the procedure adapted.
numbers: N=31 CMU students (15 list, 16 context), about 1 hour each. Accuracy 77.0% list vs 91.1% context (condition F(1,29)=7.09, p=.013). Easy 90.4 vs 93.8 (ns); medium 77.0 vs 91.0 (p=.031); hard 70.4 vs 89.9 (p=.009). Correct-trial time 28.7 s vs 24.8 s (F(1,29)=5.85, p=.022).
limits: Small N; one aviation task; one-sided Welch tests per difficulty level. The gap shrinks with practice (Exp 2).
agent_relevance: Routines stored as bare step lists are brittle. Store each step with its expected pre- and post-state so a routine can be checked and adapted.

source: Taatgen et al. (2008) model fit to Experiment 1 and prediction of Experiment 2
finding: The ACT-R model with production compilation, where only the instruction format differs between conditions, fit Experiment 1, then predicted a new Experiment 2 that added partly completed problems, some with an error.
numbers: Exp 1 fit: R2=.90 accuracy, R2=.89 log latency. Exp 2 (N=40, 20 per condition, 24 problems x 3 blocks) predicted: R2=.74 accuracy, R2=.76 log latency. Time 27.2 s list vs 23.0 s context, only marginal (F(1,38)=3.60, p=.065). Fitted: learning rate of new productions and visual attention latency.
limits: Model underestimated context-condition accuracy on problems that began with an error (it has no real error-recovery strategy). Underestimated the first few trials. Instruction effect was weaker in the longer Exp 2.
agent_relevance: Compiled routines need an explicit error-recovery path; compilation alone does not give recovery.

source: Taatgen (2005) Modeling parallelization and flexibility improvements in skill acquisition: rules for what can be merged
finding: A rule that asks perception for something cannot merge with the rule that uses the result, and two rules that call the same module (for example two key presses) cannot merge. So learning ends with rules that step from one perceptual input or motor output to the next.
numbers: Example compiled rule: IF goal is Schumacher task AND low tone detected THEN say 'one'. It came from 3 rules and 2 retrievals, compiled pairwise and then again. Compiled rules are state-independent, so behaviour becomes bottom-up (cued by the world).
limits: For complex tasks there may never be enough time to learn all the possible rules (author's note).
agent_relevance: Do not compile across a tool call: a routine can only fold steps whose inputs are already in hand. Merge points sit at tool boundaries.

source: Taatgen (2005) gradual utility learning of new compiled rules
finding: A new compiled rule starts with a very low utility and wins only after it has been re-created many times, so only frequent reasoning patterns become routine. Utility blends an inherited prior and own experience: U = (m*Uprior + n*Uexperienced)/(m+n), with m=10 by default.
numbers: m=10; the new rule effectively cannot be chosen at first; each re-creation raises Uprior. Selection is noisy, so the parent rule is still sometimes chosen (under 1% at expert level in the dual-task model).
limits: The gradual-learning assumption is needed to match human data; without it expert behaviour would arrive in a few trials. Anderson, Fincham and Douglass (1997) is cited for slow procedural learning.
agent_relevance: Promote a lesson to routine only after it recurs (a count threshold), and keep the slow parent path available as fallback.

source: Schumacher et al. (2001) perfect time-sharing, as modelled in Taatgen (2005)
finding: By Day 5 participants showed no dual-task cost in a visual-manual plus aural-vocal task. The compilation model reproduced the move from a clear dual-task cost on Day 2 to none on Day 5.
numbers: Exp 1 design: pure blocks of 45 trials; mixed blocks of 48 trials (18 dual, 30 single). Day 1 pure blocks only; Day 2: 6 pure + 8 mixed; Days 3-5: 6 pure + 10 mixed. Day 2 cost only in the aural-vocal task; gone by Day 5. Tones lasted 40 ms at 220, 880 or 3520 Hz.
limits: Human data read second-hand through the model paper (graphs, no tables). Experiment 2 needed an extra top-down order constraint to match.
agent_relevance: Practice can remove interference between sub-steps only after the steps are folded into condition-driven rules.

source: Anderson et al. (2004) CMU Aegis Simulation Program, as modelled in Taatgen (2005)
finding: In a complex radar task a hierarchical-instruction plus compilation model matched speedup but was limited by its strict hierarchy. Taatgen's weaker hierarchy (rules triggered top-down and bottom-up) let the model reorder steps and produce new strategies.
numbers: Reported experiment: 20 scenarios of 6 min over 2 days; speed and number of classified planes both improved. Model matched speedup at the level of 3 subtasks and gaze time on screen regions.
limits: Original data in Anderson et al. (2004); not opened here.
agent_relevance: Strict nested routines are inflexible. Let a compiled routine fire from state cues, not only from its parent plan.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition
finding: First full account of compilation as a single mechanism that merges task-specific declarative knowledge with domain-general rules into small task-specific rules. A model starting from instructions in declarative memory learned the Kanfer-Ackerman air traffic controller task at overall, unit-task and keystroke levels with default ACT-R parameters.
numbers: Comparison data: 65 undergraduates, 18 trials of 10 min (Ackerman & Kanfer 1994, Study 2); model compared on trials 1-10, run 5 times. Fits: planes landed r2=.97; land unit task r2=.98; queue unit task r2=.91; keystroke level r2=.87.
limits: Model faster than people on trial 1 (it starts with all visual locations and a decent strategy in declarative memory) and slower on the move and queue unit tasks (it checks before moving). Fit is to group averages, not individuals.
agent_relevance: A few generic rules plus stored instructions can yield expert routines without hand-writing the fast rules.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) over-generalisation example
finding: Compiling a rule with one remembered example creates a task-specific rule: after one success landing a DC-10 on the short runway, the model learns 'decide short runway' for DC-10. In the real task this is only sometimes right (weather and runway conditions), so the rule over-generalises.
numbers: Single-example rule. The authors say the error comes from the strategy of reusing old experience, not from compilation itself.
quote: the error of overgeneralization results from following the strategy of using old experiences and does not reflect an inherent weakness in production compilation
limits: That defence is an argument, not a test.
agent_relevance: A routine distilled from one success will be too broad. Keep the condition that made it succeed and test it on a held-out case (matches G3).

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) on individual differences and earlier KA-ATC models
finding: Earlier ACT-R work (Lee & Anderson 2000, 2001) showed expert play needs parallel cognition, perception and action. An earlier model varied working-memory capacity, production-compilation speed and psychomotor speed and reproduced Ackerman's pattern of individual-difference correlations.
numbers: Compilation speed is treated as a person-level parameter. The earlier model could not reach human performance and could not model unit tasks or keystrokes.
limits: Taken from the introduction only; the cited original studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: The speed of turning experience into routines is a tunable knob, not a constant; budget how eagerly the agent compiles.

source: Taatgen & Anderson (2002) Why do children learn to say 'broke'? A model of learning the past tense without feedback
finding: Hybrid ACT-R model starts with retrieval, analogy and do-nothing strategies, then learns new rules by specialising the analogy strategy: first 'use the stem' (about month 1), then the regular -ed rule (about month 2). The regular rule's expected outcome overtakes the zero rule around month 4. U-shaped learning appears without feedback, a vocabulary spurt or high regular-verb frequency.
numbers: About 1300 past tenses produced per month. Regular verbs are only 25-30% of verb tokens in child speech. Rule choice is stochastic: the highest expected outcome is only the most probable.
limits: Model overregularisation fades, but Adam and Sarah (Marcus et al. 1992) show no fading in the studied window; onset is more gradual in children.
agent_relevance: Compiled general rules arise from a weak method (analogy) and then compete with stored examples. Over-regularisation is the cost of a good default rule.

source: Taatgen & Anderson (2002) fit to child data
finding: Low-frequency irregular verbs fail retrieval more often and are therefore regularised more, as in children.
numbers: Correlation between parental frequency and child overregularisation: -0.34 (Marcus 1996); -0.59 in the model. Marcus (1996) overregularisation: 4.2% preschoolers, 2.5% first graders, 1% fourth graders.
limits: Model correlation is larger, perhaps because it is trained and scored on the same Francis and Kucera frequencies. Only two children (Adam, Sarah) plus Abe's individual words.
agent_relevance: Rare lessons fall back on the general rule; this is the mechanism behind confident wrong answers on exceptions.

source: Taatgen (2002) Learning rules and productions, Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science
finding: History of the idea: ACT* had four rule-learning mechanisms (proceduralization, composition, generalisation, discrimination). They were judged too unconstrained, producing too many invalid and low-utility rules. ACT-R 5 replaced proceduralization plus composition with one constrained mechanism.
numbers: ACT-R limit: each production may make only one declarative access, split in two steps (request in one rule, use in the next). Adding three numbers takes 1 rule in ACT*/Soar but 3 in ACT-R.
limits: Encyclopedia entry, a summary. The original ACT* papers (Anderson 1982, 1987) were not available.
agent_relevance: A tightly constrained compile step beats a flexible one that can emit bad rules.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R, chapter 1
finding: Lists 'specialization of task-independent cognitive strategies' as one of five modelling paradigms: general rules plus stored task facts compile into expert rules. New rules must be re-created several times before they beat the parent rule, and can then seed even faster rules.
numbers: Learned-DC10-rule: IF decide runway AND plane is DC10 AND runway dry THEN take the short runway. The model predicts planes landed and sub-task times (via Taatgen & Lee 2003).
limits: Chapter gives mechanism, not new data.
agent_relevance: Same routine pattern: general method plus remembered case gives a specific rule with explicit conditions.

source: Taatgen (2013) The nature and transfer of cognitive skills: primitive elements theory
finding: Productions are split into primitive information processing elements (PRIMs) that only compare or copy slot values. Compilation merges PRIMs that fire in sequence into larger rules. Because specifics sit in separate slots, many learned rules are task-general and reusable, which is the source of transfer.
numbers: 1,188 condition PRIMs and 504 action PRIMs; 10 input, 7 output and 14 in/out workspace slots; 1,430,586 possible pairs and 805,896,780 triples of PRIMs. New rules start with very low utility and gain it each time they are re-created.
limits: Model-only paper; the PRIM set and workspace are fixed by hand; spreading activation to pick operators is a hand-set shortcut.
agent_relevance: Store routines with their task-specific constants as parameters, so the general skeleton transfers to a new task.

source: Taatgen (2013) counting to semantic-reasoning transfer
finding: Counting and 'is a canary an animal?' share an iterate-through-memory structure. After counting is learned, the semantic model starts at an intermediate compiled rule and needs one more compilation step instead of the whole chain.
numbers: Counting uses 3 operators (Init, Step, Final). The semantic task answers 'no' on retrieval failure instead of checking an end number.
limits: Predicted by the model; no new human data for this pair.
agent_relevance: Reusable skeletons (iterate, accumulate, compare) transfer, not content.

source: Taatgen (2013) text-editor transfer vs the identical-productions model (Singley & Anderson 1985)
finding: A model with compiled task-general PRIMs fits human transfer between three editors better than counting identical productions. The biggest gain is for transfer from line editors to the screen editor Emacs.
numbers: Human / identical productions / PRIM model, % transfer. Move to line: ED->EDT 87/68/81; EDT->ED 91/75/90; line editors->Emacs 61/39/66. Plan edit in line: ED->EDT 105/90/90; EDT->ED 99/85/92; line editors->Emacs 62/27/57. Models have 23 (ED), 26 (EDT), 19 (Emacs) operators.
limits: The Singley and Anderson design has confounds: transfer measured on Day 3 vs Day 5, and fewer repetitions in slower editors. Model was fit by choosing parameters for amount and speed of learning.
agent_relevance: Transfer scales with shared sub-skills, not shared surface. Index lessons by reusable steps.

source: Taatgen (2013) far transfer: cognitive control training
finding: Training that strengthens a 'proactive' rule (input plus internal state to action) transfers to Stroop and working-memory span; training on a reactive single-task rule is predicted to hurt.
numbers: Models fit Chein and Morrison (2010; 20 sessions of complex working-memory training) and Karbach and Kray (2009; task-switching training). The model predicts Stroop interference falls after task-switching training and rises after single-task training.
limits: The predicted drop in count-span after reactive training was not found in the human data. Far transfer from cognitive training is contested in the wider literature.
agent_relevance: Practising a control strategy can bias which strategy the agent later picks. Watch for negative transfer from over-routinised habits.

source: Taatgen (2013) stated limits of compilation-based transfer
finding: For long PRIM sequences, rules may have to be relearned; the space of combinations is huge. Learning by recombination is faster than from scratch but not free.
numbers: Fixed workspace; operator retrieval uses hand-set positive associations as a shortcut for what should be learned.
limits: The theory is not tested against a case where compilation is turned off.
agent_relevance: Expect routines to need relearning when sequences are long; keep shorter reusable pieces.

source: Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice
finding: Survey of practice curves: the exponential fits better than the power function in all unaveraged data sets, and averaging biases toward a power law. The APEX function (exponential with an extra term) fit better than a general power function.
numbers: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments (13 published and 3 unpublished sources). Tasks: memory search, counting, arithmetic, visual search, motor sequences.
limits: Challenges the power law that ACT and chunking were built to explain. Authors say exponential curves follow if chunks practise only themselves, and that ACT's decaying-trace strength mechanism cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a power law of improvement when budgeting how many repetitions a lesson needs before it becomes routine.

source: Newell & Rosenbloom (1981) Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice (as described by Heathcote et al. 2000)
finding: Chunking theory: solved sub-problems become chunks; reaction time follows a power function of practice. Power fit beat exponential in every comparison, on mostly averaged data.
numbers: Only one task in the 1981 chapter was unaveraged. Seibel (1963) data: 1,023 key-press combinations, first 75 blocks of subject J.K.
limits: Original chapter not opened; claims come from Heathcote et al. The theory predicts a decreasing rate of learning, not exactly a power law.
agent_relevance: Chunking is the Soar parent of compilation; compilation works at the grain of single steps.

source: Anderson (1982) Acquisition of cognitive skill and Anderson (1987) Skill acquisition: compilation of weak-method problem solutions (as described in Taatgen & Lee 2003 and Taatgen 2013)
finding: Three stages (cognitive, associative, autonomous; Fitts 1964) are recast as a shift from declarative knowledge interpreted by general rules to compiled procedural knowledge. Weak methods such as analogy are the starting point; specialisation produces fast task-specific rules.
numbers: Anderson (1982) treated the log-linear power law as the signature of skill acquisition. ACT* also had generalisation, discrimination and strength mechanisms.
limits: Primary papers are closed access; not opened. Description is second-hand.
agent_relevance: The old two-store view (facts replaced by rules) is the same as our lesson-to-routine path.

source: Anderson, Fincham & Douglass (1997) The role of examples and rules in the acquisition of a cognitive skill (cited in Taatgen 2005)
finding: Cited as evidence that procedural learning is slow and gradual, which motivates giving new compiled rules a low starting utility.
numbers: No figures were read.
limits: Not opened; cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: Routines should take time to displace stored examples.

source: Singley & Anderson (1985) The transfer of text-editing skill (as described in Taatgen 2013)
finding: Productions as the unit of transfer: overlap in rules between text editors predicted transfer between them, but not all of it.
numbers: 6-day experiment, 3 h/day, six conditions (one typing control); line editors ED and EDT, screen editor Emacs. Observed line-to-screen transfer 62%; identical-productions model gave 33%. Kieras and Bovair (1986) predicted learning time of extensions from the extra number of productions.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Fixed rule counting under-predicts transfer; reuse is partial, not all-or-none.

source: Logan (1988) instance theory compared with chunking and compilation (as described in Taatgen et al. 2008)
finding: Three accounts of speedup: instance theory (store whole solved problems; race retrieval against an algorithm), chunking (store sub-goal results), compilation (merge single steps). They differ mainly in grain size.
numbers: Taatgen et al. say none of the three addresses flexibility or robustness directly: specialisation implies the knowledge cannot be used on unseen cases.
limits: Comparison written by compilation proponents; Logan's own paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Case memory vs rule memory is a choice of grain; our lesson store is the instance route, our routines the rule route.

source: Gianferrara, Betts & Anderson (2021) Cognitive and motor skill transfer across speeds: a video game study
finding: An ACT-R model with production compilation (and control tuning) predicts transfer across game speeds. Authors call compilation a general skill acquisition process within tasks, but never switched it off.
numbers: N=80 MTurk (82 recruited, 2 excluded), 20 per transfer condition. Transfer to high speed: humans median 131%, model 68%; to low speed: humans 76%, model 82%. Best fit: 2 trackers, RMSE 304 points (BIC 686) vs 479 (BIC 741) with one tracker.
limits: Compilation not manipulated, so its share of transfer is inferred. Base-level learning off. Model relies only on feedback and shows a reset spike at transfer that humans lack. Only 20 per cell. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Even a recent model leaves the compilation claim untested by ablation; treat it as plausible, not shown.

source: Ji, van Rij & Taatgen (2025) Simulating procedural discovery in early language acquisition
finding: A recent PRIMs model that sets automatic compilation aside and learns procedures through operator-to-context association strength instead.
numbers: Study 1: 4 trisyllabic words, 200 training patterns, 10 test patterns, 100 runs per condition. High-efficiency models: words 442 ms faster than part-words; part-words 515 ms faster than non-words; low-efficiency models 3188 ms longer on task. Action time 300 ms vs 50 ms for low vs high efficiency.
limits: Only the first part of the article was read. Age effects moderately reproduced for on-task time and not for operator latency.
agent_relevance: An alternative to compilation for building routines: strengthen operator-in-context links.

source: Taatgen (2017) Towards cognitive architectures with multiple levels of abstraction
finding: Argues ACT-R lacks representations for compositionality: people can carry out a novel task at once if its parts are mastered. Proposes layers (neurons, PRIM-like rules, tasks) with learning between layers.
numbers: Examples include a tone-to-number aural-vocal task and two novel mini-tasks; no new data.
limits: Position paper; only the first pages were read.
agent_relevance: Compose new tasks from already-compiled parts: the routine library should be combinable.

source: Unnamed authors (2026) AI-augmented ACT-R modeling in real interfaces (EVisiTor)
finding: LLMs convert written instructions into ACT-R declarative chunks, but the paper states the LLM does not write the model or create production rules, so compilation stays with ACT-R.
numbers: 14 instructions parsed by 6 LLMs: target accuracy averaged 94.6% (Gemini-3.5-Flash) and 92.3% (GPT-5.5). 281 declarative structures produced. Excel task: RMSE 29.19 s to 17.37 s (-40%); total 732.6 s vs human 715.4 s vs 391.9 s for a perfect user (21 humans, 142 runs per cell). Windows tasks: broad-instruction exact agreement 42.5-63.6% without UIA.
limits: No production-compilation result in this paper. Only the first 100,000 characters were read. One demonstration per Windows task; hosted LLM endpoints may drift.
agent_relevance: Closest 2026 pairing of LLMs with ACT-R: the LLM parses instructions, the architecture does the lesson-to-routine step. Keep the compile step in code.
